Train the hybrid clock on a reference set

Source: R/train.R
train_clock.Rd

Fits one Cubist model (Quinlan 1993; Kuhn and Quinlan 2023) per target, from the summaries of each simulated sample to its true history, and gives each estimate an interval by split-conformal calibration (Vovk et al. 2005; Lei et al. 2018). The simulated runs are divided into three sets so that no run informs more than one step: one to fit the models, one to calibrate the intervals, and one to test the finished estimator.

Usage

train_clock(
  reference,
  targets = c("hybrid_age_both", "hybrid_age_rare", "backcrosses", "arriving",
    "arrival_rate"),
  level = 0.9,
  split = c(fit = 0.6, calibrate = 0.2, test = 0.2),
  max_rows = 40000,
  committees = 20,
  bins = 8,
  intervals = c("normalized", "binned", "cqr"),
  cores = 1,
  seed = 1
)

Arguments

reference

Output of build_reference().

targets

Which parts of the history to estimate. See simulate_hybrid_zone() for definitions. arriving and arrival_rate describe new hybridization: whether pure animals of the rarer species are still arriving, and if so what share of breeders they make up per generation.

level

Interval coverage.

split

Shares of runs used to fit, calibrate and test.

max_rows

Most samples used to fit each model.

committees

Number of Cubist committees.

bins

Number of ranges of the estimate within which intervals are calibrated.

intervals

How intervals are made: "binned" (split-conformal residuals within ranges of the estimate and by sample type) or "cqr" (conformalized quantile regression: a quantile forest gives each sample its own interval from its summaries, widened on calibration runs to the stated coverage; Romano et al. 2019), or "normalized" (intervals centred on the estimate, scaled by a forest's prediction of each sample's typical error, and calibrated on held-out runs; Papadopoulos et al. 2011).

cores

Number of processes (targets are fitted in parallel).

seed

Random seed.

Value

An object of class hybridclock_model: the fitted models, the interval calibration, the features used, the reference settings and a validation table of accuracy on the test runs.

Details

New hybridization is estimated in two parts. arriving is the probability that pure animals of the rarer species are still arriving (over the three generations before sampling), from a probability forest (Wright and Ziegler 2017) trained on equal numbers of histories with and without arrivals, so the prior odds are even. Its probabilities are then recalibrated on the calibration runs by logistic regression on the forest's log-odds, the estimated hybrid age and their interaction (Platt 1999), because the same summaries mean different things in young and old swarms: in a young swarm, pure founders still form new hybrids without any arrivals. arrival_rate is the rate if they are, from a Cubist model trained only on histories with arrivals.

Ages and rates are modeled on a log scale (log(age), log(1 + backcrosses), log(arrival_rate)). Fitting and calibration sets are balanced so that every range of the target is equally common; otherwise the most common ages in the reference set pull estimates toward them. Intervals are calibrated separately within ranges of the estimate (Mondrian conformal prediction), so that young and old estimates each get intervals of the right width. Coverage is guaranteed on average over histories like those in the reference set, which is why its settings should match the study system.

References

Kuhn M, Quinlan R (2023) Cubist: Rule- and instance-based regression modeling. R package.

Lei J, G'Sell M, Rinaldo A, Tibshirani RJ, Wasserman L (2018) Distribution-free predictive inference for regression. Journal of the American Statistical Association 113:1094-1111.

Quinlan JR (1993) Combining instance-based and model-based learning. Proceedings of the Tenth International Conference on Machine Learning, 236-243.

Vovk V, Gammerman A, Shafer G (2005) Algorithmic Learning in a Random World. Springer.

Platt J (1999) Probabilistic outputs for support vector machines and comparisons to regularized likelihood methods. In: Advances in Large Margin Classifiers, MIT Press, 61-74.

Wright MN, Ziegler A (2017) ranger: A fast implementation of random forests for high dimensional data in C++ and R. Journal of Statistical Software 77:1-17.

Examples

# \donttest{
ref <- build_reference(n_sims = 150, generations = 12, n_markers = 200, breeders = c(20, 100))
clock <- train_clock(ref, targets = "hybrid_age_both", committees = 5)
clock
#> hybridclock model: hybrid_age_both 
#>   reference: 200 markers, 0 shared loci, samples of 20 animals, breeders 20 to 100 
#>   90% intervals; accuracy on held-out runs:
#>           target typical_error coverage
#>  hybrid_age_both          0.12     0.95
#>   individual classes are used when at least 90% of hybrids fit an early class
# }
